passage: Dear diary, I'm Disha, and I got my science test back today. I failed. I sat at my desk with my face hot, hoping nobody would look. At break I went to the corner by the water tank so no one would see me. Then Mehak came. She said, "I didn't do well last unit either. I cried in the toilet. Want to study together?" I nearly cried right there. We made a list of the chapters I missed, and she said we could go through them on Saturday at her house. I still feel sad about the mark, but the sadness is smaller. It's not just my problem now, it's ours.

qa.q: Where did Disha go at break so nobody would see?
qa.a: Disha went to the corner by the water tank.

qa.q: What made Disha nearly cry when Mehak spoke to Disha?
qa.a: Disha felt relief and gratitude at not being alone, since Mehak said she had struggled too and offered to study together.

qa.q: How does studying together change failure for Disha?
qa.a: It turns it from a private shame into a shared problem with a plan, a list of chapters and a Saturday to work on them.

qa.q: Why might Mehak have chosen to tell Disha about crying in the toilet?
qa.a: To show she understands, since she has been in the same place and does not judge.

grounding: A child who failed a test feels less alone when a friend shares her own struggle and offers to study together.

passage:
Sonali sat on the steps of the village temple with her failed English paper in her lap. Seventeen out of fifty. The goats nibbled the grass below, not interested.
Lalit, her friend from the next farm, sat down beside her and glanced at the paper. "Seventeen? I got nineteen last year. I cried in the cowshed."
Sonali looked up. "You? You're good at everything."
"Not English. Tenses make my head spin. Want to do it together? Master-ji said we can use the panchayat library after four."
For the next month they sat at the library's wobbly table every evening, testing each other from a torn grammar book. When Sonali got a sentence right, Lalit clapped. When he forgot, she corrected him.
In the next test Sonali got thirty-four. Lalit got thirty-six. They bought one orange ice lolly and shared it.

qa.q: What did Sonali get in her English paper?
How did Sonali feel when Lalit said he had also struggled?
qa.a: Surprised and less alone, since she had thought he was good at everything.

qa.q: How did studying together turn the failure around?
qa.a: They tested each other every evening at the library, making her failure a shared problem with a plan, and both improved.

qa.q: How might Lalit feel helping Sonali?
qa.a: Glad and understanding, since he remembered crying over his own low marks.

grounding: A girl who failed a test is comforted when a friend says he struggled too and offers to study together.

passage:
Amara pushed her history test into her locker so hard the door bounced back. Five out of twenty. Her family had only been in Madrid a year, and all the dates and kings swam together.
Diego leaned on the next locker. "Bad?"
She nodded, not trusting her voice.
"Last year I failed maths twice," he said. "My mum cried more than I did. Then my cousin made me flashcards, and it got better." He shrugged. "Want to do history flashcards? I'm terrible at dates too."
That afternoon they sat at the back table of his aunt's cafe, making cards with drawings: a king with a crown of oranges, a ship made of numbers. They quizzed each other over hot chocolate.
Amara walked home feeling lighter. The failure hadn't vanished, but it had become a project for two.

qa.q: What score did Amara get in the history test?
How did Amara feel after the afternoon at the cafe?
qa.a: Lighter and less alone, since the failure had become a shared project.

qa.q: What made Diego's offer so helpful?
qa.a: He admitted his own failures and offered a concrete plan: making flashcards together.

qa.q: How might Diego see Amara's failed test?
qa.a: As something he understands from failing maths twice himself, not something to judge.

grounding: A girl upset about a failed test is helped by a friend who admits he struggled too and offers to study with her.
